claim: Dendritic spikes (dSpikes) can be mediated by several channel types including Nav channels, Cav channels, and NMDAR channels.
source: Several channel types can mediate dendritically initiated spikes (dSpikes), which may impact information processing and storage across multiple timescales
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous literature throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dendritic spikes mediated by Nav channels (blocked by a low concentration of TTX) are required for long-term potentiation (LTP) in the distal apical dendrites of hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: We show here that dSpikes mediated by Nav channels (blocked by a low concentration of TTX) are required for long-term potentiation (LTP) in the distal apical dendrites of hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing that 20 nM TTX blocks LTP (Figure 3).

claim: Fast Nav channel-mediated dSpikes (Na-dSpikes) contribute to LTP induction by promoting large, transient, localized increases in intracellular calcium concentration near the calcium-conducting pores of NMDAR and L-type Cav channels.
source: Furthermore, imaging, simulations, and buffering experiments all support a model whereby fast Nav channel-mediated dSpikes (Na-dSpikes) contribute to LTP induction by promoting large, transient, localized increases in intracellular calcium concentration near the calcium-conducting pores of NMDAR and L-type Cav channels.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging experiments (Figure 7), computational modeling (Figure 8), and calcium buffering experiments (Figure 9).

claim: Na-dSpikes contribute to memory formation via their role in long-lasting synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, in addition to contributing to rapid neural processing, Na-dSpikes are likely to contribute to memory formation via their role in long-lasting synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the demonstrated role of Na-dSpikes in LTP, which is believed to be a cellular mechanism for memory.

claim: Hebbian remodeling of neural circuits is the leading candidate mechanism for learning in the brain.
source: Hebbian remodeling of neural circuits, encapsulated by the phrase 'neurons that fire together wire together', is the leading candidate mechanism for learning in the brain (Shatz, 1992; Cooper, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Postsynaptic calcium entry is believed to be a critical activator of the biochemical steps necessary for increases in synaptic strength.
source: Both of these effects mediate postsynaptic calcium entry, which is believed to be a critical activator of the biochemical steps necessary for increases in synaptic strength (Madison et al., 1991; Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Blackstone and Sheng, 2002; Cavazzini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Hippocampal place cells can be recruited to participate in the network representation of a spatial map even when initially silent.
source: Interestingly, hippocampal place cells behave in a manner suggestive of a form of Hebbian LTP that may not require postsynaptic action potential firing: many cells are silent when the animal first goes to a new place, and then they are recruited to participate in the network representation of the spatial map (Frank et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frank et al., 2004.

claim: Hippocampal neurons receive spatially tuned synaptic inputs even when they are silent.
source: Consistent with this idea, hippocampal neurons receive spatially tuned synaptic inputs even when they are silent (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: LTP at PP→CA1tuft synapses requires strong synaptic activation.
source: At synapses from the perforant path (PP; which carries predominantly spatial information from the entorhinal cortex) to the distal apical tuft of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons, LTP requires strong synaptic activation, and LTP induction can have a significant impact on the output of CA1 neurons (Colbert and Levy, 1993; Remondes and Schuman, 2002; Ahmed and Siegelbaum, 2009; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: LTP at PP→CA1tuft synapses does not require backpropagating action potentials (bAPs).
source: In previous work, we showed that LTP at these synapses does not require bAPs; rather, LTP is correlated with the initiation of dSpikes, which often do not trigger action potential firing and bAPs (Golding and Spruston, 1998; Golding et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Three types of dSpikes have been described: dendritic sodium spikes (Na-dSpikes), dendritic calcium spikes (Ca-dSpikes), and dendritic NMDA spikes (NMDA-dSpikes).
source: Three types of dSpikes have been described, which have been named according to the primary channel type supporting the regenerative event: dendritic sodium spikes (Na-dSpikes) and dendritic calcium spikes (Ca-dSpikes) are mediated primarily by voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels and Cav channels, respectively, while dendritic NMDA spikes (NMDA-dSpikes) are mediated primarily by NMDAR channels (Schwartzkroin and Slawsky, 1977; Andreasen and Lambert, 1995; Schiller et al., 1997; Golding et al., 1999; Larkum et al., 1999; Spruston, 2008; Larkum et al., 2009; Major et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: NMDAR and Cav channels contribute to the induction of LTP at PP-CA1 synapses.
source: NMDAR and Cav channels are known to contribute to the induction of LTP at PP-CA1 synapses (Golding et al., 2002; Takahashi and Magee, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The IC50 of TTX on Nav channels has been estimated as 6–10 nM in dissociated hippocampal neurons.
source: The IC50 of TTX on Nav channels has been estimated as 6–10 nM in dissociated hippocampal neurons (Kaneda et al., 1989; Madeja, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bath application of 20 nM TTX had no significant effect on PP→CA1tuft EPSPs in response to either single-shock or high-frequency burst stimulation across a wide range of stimulus intensities.
source: Bath application of low TTX had no significant effect on PP → CA1tuft EPSPs in response to either type of stimulation, across a wide range of stimulus intensities resulting in EPSPs from ∼3 mV (single shock) up to ∼27 mV (high-frequency burst; Figure 1B–G; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 20 nM TTX raised the voltage threshold and reduced action potential amplitude slightly when action potentials were evoked by somatic current injection.
source: Consistent with this result and with the notion of a high safety factor for action potential initiation in the axon (Coombs et al., 1957; Mainen et al., 1995; Raastad and Shepherd, 2003; Clark et al., 2005; Khaliq and Raman, 2006; Kole and Stuart, 2008; Hu and Jonas, 2014), low TTX did not block action potential firing in response to somatic current injection, though it did raise the voltage threshold and reduce action potential amplitude slightly, as expected from a reduction of Nav channel availability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 1—source data 2; see also Mackenzie and Murphy, 1998; Magee and Carruth, 1999; Fan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous literature.

claim: 20 nM TTX only affected antidromic action potential firing at low stimulus intensities, but not at high stimulus intensities.
source: In addition, we tested the effects of low TTX on action potentials evoked by repeated bursts of antidromic stimulation of CA1 axons and found that low TTX only affected antidromic action potential firing at low stimulus intensities. At high stimulus intensities, antidromic spikes were not blocked by low TTX (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three types of regenerative dendritic responses were observed: bAPs, large dSpikes, and small dSpikes (spikelets).
source: Consistent with previous results (Golding and Spruston, 1998; Golding et al., 2002; Losonczy and Magee, 2006), we observed three types of regenerative dendritic responses: (1) bAPs, (2) large dSpikes, and (3) small dSpikes (also known as 'spikelets').
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous literature.

claim: Large dSpikes reflect dSpikes that have propagated actively from their initiation site to the recording site.
source: Large dSpikes reflect dSpikes that have propagated actively from their initiation site to the recording site.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the understanding of dendritic spike propagation.

claim: Small dSpikes (spikelets) result from dSpikes that fall below threshold for active propagation and then propagate passively to the recording electrode.
source: However, dSpikes can fall below threshold for active propagation (often because of large impedance drops at branch points) and then propagate passively to the recording electrode, where they appear as small dSpikes (spikelets) (Golding and Spruston, 1998; Golding et al., 2002; Jarsky et al., 2005; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Katz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the presence of 20 nM TTX, both the number and the amplitude of large-amplitude dendritic events (bAPs and large dSpikes) were reduced.
source: In the presence of low TTX, both the number and the amplitude of large-amplitude dendritic events (i.e., bAPs and large dSpikes, all with amplitudes >40 mV; see 'Materials and methods') were reduced (control: amplitude = 56.2 ± 1.8 mV, n = 39 events; low TTX: amplitude = 44.8 ± 1.7 mV, n = 17 events; p < 10−4 by Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Application of 20 nM TTX dramatically reduced the number of small dSpikes (spikelets).
source: We found that application of low TTX dramatically reduced the number of small dSpikes defined by all confidence levels in this range (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—source data 1; see Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for all small dSpikes identified by the 99% confidence level; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 20 nM TTX is an effective inhibitor of dSpikes generated in response to TBS of the PP.
source: As both large dSpikes and small dSpikes (spikelets) reflect the presence of dSpikes initiated in the tuft dendrites, and both were inhibited by low TTX, we conclude that low TTX is an effective inhibitor of dSpikes generated in response to TBS of the PP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing inhibition of both large and small dSpikes by TTX.

claim: The magnitude of PP→CA1tuft LTP was similar when TBS was paired with somatic current injections (TBSx3+Current) or delivered with somatic voltage clamp (TBSx3+SomaticVC).
source: The magnitude of PP → CA1tuft LTP was similar in these two conditions (Figure 3B–E; TBSx3+Current, potentiation ratio = 1.63 ± 0.16, n = 9; TBSx3+SomaticVC, potentiation ratio = 1.53 ± 0.07, n = 9; p = 1.00 by one-way ANOVA; Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: Action potential firing did not contribute to LTP induction at PP→CA1tuft synapses.
source: The magnitude of PP → CA1tuft LTP was similar in these two conditions (Figure 3B–E; TBSx3+Current, potentiation ratio = 1.63 ± 0.16, n = 9; TBSx3+SomaticVC, potentiation ratio = 1.53 ± 0.07, n = 9; p = 1.00 by one-way ANOVA; Figure 3—source data 1), suggesting that action potential firing did not contribute to LTP induction at these synapses (see also Golding et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing similar LTP with and without action potential firing, supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PP→CA1tuft LTP was blocked completely in the presence of 20 nM TTX under both TBSx3+Current and TBSx3+SomaticVC conditions.
source: Under both conditions, PP → CA1tuft LTP was blocked completely in the presence of low TTX (Figure 3C–E; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: PP→CA1tuft LTP was reduced approximately 50% by blocking NMDARs.
source: We previously showed that PP → CA1tuft LTP was reduced ∼50% by blocking NMDARs, ∼50% by blocking L-, T-, and R-type Cav channels, and almost completely by blocking NMDARs and Cav channels together (Golding et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: PP→CA1tuft LTP was reduced approximately 50% by blocking L-, T-, and R-type Cav channels.
source: We previously showed that PP → CA1tuft LTP was reduced ∼50% by blocking NMDARs, ∼50% by blocking L-, T-, and R-type Cav channels, and almost completely by blocking NMDARs and Cav channels together (Golding et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: PP→CA1tuft LTP was blocked almost completely by blocking NMDARs and Cav channels together.
source: We previously showed that PP → CA1tuft LTP was reduced ∼50% by blocking NMDARs, ∼50% by blocking L-, T-, and R-type Cav channels, and almost completely by blocking NMDARs and Cav channels together (Golding et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The effects of Cav channel blockers on PP→CA1tuft LTP were attributable to blocking L-type Cav channels, but not blocking T-, R-, or other types of Cav channels.
source: We confirmed these results here and showed further that the effects of Cav channel blockers were attributable to blocking L-type Cav channels (with 10 µM nimodipine), but not blocking T-, R-, or other types of Cav channels (with 50 µM Ni2+; Figure 4; Figure 4—source data 1; see also Remy and Spruston, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and a citation to previous work.

claim: 10 µM nimodipine had no effect on synaptic responses, either before or after the induction of PP→CA1tuft LTP.
source: Furthermore, 10 µM nimodipine had no effect on synaptic responses, either before or after the induction of PP → CA1tuft LTP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—source data 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: L-type Cav channels are involved in the induction rather than the expression of PP→CA1tuft LTP.
source: Furthermore, 10 µM nimodipine had no effect on synaptic responses, either before or after the induction of PP → CA1tuft LTP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—source data 2), suggesting that L-type Cav channels are involved in the induction rather than the expression of LTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no effect of nimodipine on synaptic responses.

claim: NMDAR and L-type Cav channels are the two main sources of calcium entry during LTP induction by TBS of PP→CA1tuft synapses.
source: These results suggest that NMDAR and L-type Cav (L-Cav) channels are the two main sources of calcium entry during LTP induction by TBS of PP → CA1tuft synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that blocking these channels inhibits LTP.

claim: 20 nM TTX blocked large and small dSpikes.
source: As described above, low TTX blocked large and small dSpikes (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 50 µM AP5 did not block a large dSpike observed in dendritic recordings.
source: In one of the two dendritic recordings where we observed inhibition of a clear large dSpike by low TTX, we subsequently washed out TTX and applied 50 µM AP5, which did not block the large dSpike (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 20 nM TTX had almost no effect on the slow depolarization produced by each burst of PP→CA1tuft EPSPs in response to TBS.
source: By contrast, low TTX had almost no effect on the slow depolarization produced by each burst of PP → CA1tuft EPSPs in response to TBS, whereas 50 µM AP5 had a much greater effect on the slow depolarization associated with each burst.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 50 µM AP5 had a much greater effect on the slow depolarization associated with each burst than 20 nM TTX.
source: By contrast, low TTX had almost no effect on the slow depolarization produced by each burst of PP → CA1tuft EPSPs in response to TBS, whereas 50 µM AP5 had a much greater effect on the slow depolarization associated with each burst.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The fast depolarization associated with Na-dSpikes is more important for the induction of PP→CA1tuft LTP than the slow synaptic depolarization mediated solely by EPSPs.
source: Because low TTX was a more potent inhibitor of PP → CA1tuft LTP than 50 µM AP5 (Figure 4F), these results suggest that the fast depolarization associated with Na-dSpikes is more important for the induction of PP → CA1tuft LTP than the slow synaptic depolarization mediated solely by EPSPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of TTX and AP5 on LTP and on dendritic depolarization.

claim: A modified TBS pattern consisting of only 2 stimuli in each burst (2-stim TBSx3) induced LTP at PP→CA1tuft synapses of approximately the same magnitude as TBSx3 protocols consisting of 5 stimuli (5-stim) in each burst.
source: This 2-stim protocol induced LTP at PP → CA1tuft synapses of approximately the same magnitude as various TBSx3 protocols consisting of 5 stimuli (5-stim) in each burst (Figure 6B,C; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The 2-stim TBSx3 protocol yielded PP→CA1tuft LTP of 82% of the average LTP induced by all variants of the 5-stim TBSx3 protocol, despite a greatly reduced integral of the slow depolarization (27% of that with 5-stim TBSx3).
source: The 2-stim TBSx3 protocol yielded PP → CA1tuft LTP of 82% of the average LTP induced by all variants of the 5-stim TBSx3 protocol, despite a greatly reduced integral of the slow depolarization (27% of that with 5-stim TBSx3; Figure 6D,E; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 20 nM TTX blocks PP→CA1tuft LTP by inhibiting fast Na-dSpikes, with minimal effect on the slow synaptic depolarization induced by each high-frequency burst during TBS.
source: Collectively, the results above indicate that low TTX blocks PP → CA1tuft LTP by inhibiting fast Na-dSpikes, with minimal effect on the slow synaptic depolarization induced by each high-frequency burst during TBS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing differential effects of TTX on dSpikes and slow depolarization.

claim: Burst stimulation of the PP resulted in clear ΔG/R responses (79 ± 14%, n = 17 cells), which were significantly reduced by 50 µM AP5.
source: Burst stimulation of the PP resulted in clear ΔG/R responses (79 ± 14%, n = 17 cells), which were significantly reduced by 50 µM AP5 (Figure 7B; Figure 7—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: 20 nM TTX was far less potent at inhibiting intracellular calcium elevations than 50 µM AP5.
source: Importantly, however, low TTX was far less potent at inhibiting intracellular calcium elevations than 50 µM AP5 (Figure 7B,C; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The effectiveness of 20 nM TTX as a blocker of LTP cannot be explained by its effect on the measured dendritic calcium signals.
source: This result was surprising, given that it is opposite to what one would expect from the result that low TTX was a far more potent inhibitor of PP → CA1tuft LTP than 50 µM AP5. This suggests that the effectiveness of low TTX as a blocker of LTP cannot be explained by its effect on the measured dendritic calcium signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between the effects of TTX on LTP and on bulk calcium signals.

claim: The computational model was able to reproduce the effects of 20 nM TTX and 50 µM AP5 on dSpikes and EPSPs recorded from the distal apical trunk.
source: The model was able to reproduce the effects of low TTX (simulated by 50% reduction of Nav channel conductance) and 50 µM AP5 (simulated by complete block of NMDARs) on dSpikes and EPSPs recorded from the distal apical trunk (Figure 8A–C; Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The computational model was able to reproduce the effects of TTX and AP5 on dendritic calcium transients.
source: The simulations were also able to reproduce the effects of TTX and AP5 on dendritic calcium transients (Figure 7), as measured by the modeled increase in the concentration of simulated calcium-bound OGB-1 ([Ca2+]OGB) in response to burst activation of simulated synapses (Figure 8B,C; Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the computational model, the largest instantaneous calcium currents (ICa) through NMDAR and L-Cav channels were mediated by locally generated Na-dSpikes.
source: Simulations at the synapses revealed that the largest instantaneous calcium currents (ICa) through NMDAR and L-Cav channels were mediated by locally generated Na-dSpikes, owing to efficient relief of magnesium block of NMDAR channels and strong activation of L-Cav channels, respectively (Figure 8D; Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: A large, rapid, Na-dSpike-mediated component of calcium entry may produce transient, localized increases in intracellular calcium concentration that are essential for the induction of TBS-induced PP→CA1tuft LTP.
source: These simulations, combined with the experimental results, suggest that a large, rapid, Na-dSpike-mediated component of calcium entry may produce transient, localized increases in intracellular calcium concentration that are essential for the induction of TBS-induced PP → CA1tuft LTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling and experimental results.

claim: 10 µM nimodipine did not have a significant effect on dendritic calcium responses during burst stimulation of the PP.
source: Indeed, we found that 10 µM nimodipine did not have a significant effect on dendritic calcium responses during burst stimulation of the PP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 8—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: L-Cav channels contribute to the induction of PP→CA1tuft LTP by mediating increases in localized calcium near the channel pores rather than in dendritic bulk calcium.
source: This result is consistent with our hypothesis that L-Cav channels contribute to the induction of PP → CA1tuft LTP by mediating increases in localized calcium near the channel pores rather than in dendritic bulk calcium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no effect of nimodipine on bulk calcium signals.

claim: Only a high concentration of BAPTA (10 mM) blocked PP→CA1tuft LTP, while lower concentrations of BAPTA (0.5 mM) or EGTA (0.5 mM and 10 mM) did not.
source: We predicted that only a high concentration of BAPTA should buffer intracellular calcium increases rapidly and effectively enough to block PP → CA1tuft LTP, and this was indeed found to be the case (Figure 9; Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: NMDAR and L-Cav channels contribute to the induction of TBS-induced PP→CA1tuft LTP by mediating calcium influx.
source: These results suggest that NMDAR and L-Cav channels contribute to the induction of TBS-induced PP → CA1tuft LTP by mediating calcium influx
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that blocking these channels inhibits LTP.

claim: It is the large, transient, localized increases in intracellular calcium concentration mediated by Na-dSpikes that are critical for PP→CA1tuft LTP.
source: These results suggest that NMDAR and L-Cav channels contribute to the induction of TBS-induced PP → CA1tuft LTP by mediating calcium influx, and are consistent with the hypothesis that it is the large, transient, localized increases in intracellular calcium concentration mediated by Na-dSpikes that are critical for this form of LTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from calcium buffering experiments and computational modeling.

claim: The experiments support a causal role of dendritic Nav channels, by triggering Na-dSpikes, in the induction of PP→CA1tuft LTP.
source: In summary, the experiments presented here argue for a critical, causal role of dendritic Nav channels, by triggering Na-dSpikes, in the induction of PP → CA1tuft LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that blocking Nav channels with TTX blocks LTP.

claim: Na-dSpikes have a role in the rapid, moment-to-moment processing of internal and external information by influencing synaptic integration.
source: With this conclusion, we have now established possible functional roles for Na-dSpikes not only in the rapid, moment-to-moment processing of internal and external information (by influencing synaptic integration; Golding and Spruston, 1998; Jarsky et al., 2005; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Katz et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Na-dSpikes have a role in the long-term storage of information by a Na-dSpike-dependent form of LTP.
source: With this conclusion, we have now established possible functional roles for Na-dSpikes not only in the rapid, moment-to-moment processing of internal and external information (by influencing synaptic integration; Golding and Spruston, 1998; Jarsky et al., 2005; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Katz et al., 2009), but also in the long-term storage of this information (by a Na-dSpike-dependent form of LTP).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in this study.

claim: Dendritic Nav channels were previously known to contribute to the cellular basis of memory by mediating forms of LTP that require action potential backpropagation.
source: Dendritic Nav channels were previously known to contribute to the cellular basis of memory by mediating forms of LTP that require action potential backpropagation.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Dendritic Nav channels can contribute to memory formation via a critical role for Na-dSpikes in some forms of LTP.
source: Our results suggest that dendritic Nav channels can also contribute to memory formation via a critical role for Na-dSpikes in some forms of LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in this study.

claim: The form of LTP studied here is Hebbian on a finer spatial scale, for which the rule can be rephrased as 'neurites that fire together wire together'.
source: Our view is that this form of LTP is Hebbian on a finer spatial scale, for which the rule can be rephrased as 'neurites that fire together wire together'.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of Hebbian learning theory.

claim: Dendritic Nav channels play a central role in determining which postsynaptic neurites fire.
source: Dendritic Nav channels play a central role in the cellular implementation of this rule, by determining which postsynaptic neurites fire.
evidence: This is an inference based on the demonstrated role of Nav channels in generating Na-dSpikes.

claim: The calcium influx during Na-dSpikes (via NMDAR and L-Cav channels) is vigorous and brief, whereas the calcium influx during slow synaptic depolarization (via NMDAR channels) is smaller, but longer lasting.
source: A simple explanation, supported by our modeling (Figure 8) and the subsequent experiments (Figure 9), is that the calcium influx during Na-dSpikes (via NMDAR and L-Cav channels) is vigorous and brief, whereas the calcium influx during slow synaptic depolarization (via NMDAR channels) is smaller, but longer lasting.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling and experimental data.

claim: The vigorous and brief calcium entry during Na-dSpikes is more critical for the induction of PP→CA1tuft LTP than the longer-lasting calcium entry during slow synaptic depolarization.
source: Although the latter ultimately contributes more to the total amount of calcium entry during a burst and comprises the vast majority of the bulk calcium measured with dendritic calcium imaging, the vigorous and brief calcium entry during Na-dSpikes is more critical for the induction of PP → CA1tuft LTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that TTX blocks LTP more effectively than AP5, despite having less effect on bulk calcium.

claim: During TBS, Na-dSpikes produce the largest voltage excursions and maximize ICa through both NMDAR and L-Cav channels.
source: During TBS, Na-dSpikes produce the largest voltage excursions and maximize ICa through both NMDAR and L-Cav channels (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 10.

claim: The large ICa caused by the Na-dSpike produces a brief, high calcium concentration near the mouth of the channels, which will quickly diffuse away and contribute modestly to the bulk calcium concentration in the rest of the dendritic spine and shaft.
source: The large ICa caused by the Na-dSpike produces a brief, high calcium concentration near the mouth of the channels, which will quickly diffuse away and contribute modestly to the bulk calcium concentration in the rest of the dendritic spine and shaft.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of calcium dynamics and diffusion.

claim: Most of the bulk calcium is generated by the smaller, but longer-lasting flux of calcium through the NMDAR channels activated during the slow synaptic depolarization.
source: On the other hand, most of the bulk calcium is generated by the smaller, but longer-lasting flux of calcium through the NMDAR channels activated during the slow synaptic depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of calcium dynamics and the experimental data.

claim: The calcium concentration near the mouth of the channels is proportional to the instantaneous amplitude of ICa, while the bulk calcium concentration is proportional to the time integral of ICa through the calcium-permeable channels.
source: The calcium concentration near the mouth of the channels is proportional to the instantaneous amplitude of ICa, while the bulk calcium concentration is proportional to the time integral of ICa through the calcium-permeable channels (Augustine et al., 2003; Eggermann et al., 2012; Tadross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on calcium dynamics.

claim: The efficacy of 20 nM TTX as a blocker of LTP by inhibiting Na-dSpikes could be explained by the existence of a calcium sensor near the channels that triggers a series of LTP-inducing biochemical events.
source: The efficacy of low TTX as a blocker of LTP by inhibiting Na-dSpikes could be explained by the existence of a calcium sensor near the channels that triggers a series of LTP-inducing biochemical events (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental results.

claim: The affinity and co-operativity of the calcium sensor would have to be matched to the spatiotemporal features of the calcium concentration profiles near the mouths of NMDAR and L-Cav channels in response to TBS.
source: The affinity and co-operativity of the calcium sensor would have to be matched to the spatiotemporal features of the calcium concentration profiles near the mouths of NMDAR and L-Cav channels in response to TBS.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for the proposed calcium sensor mechanism.

claim: The affinity of the calcium sensor would need to be relatively low, in order to respond only to the high calcium concentration near the calcium-conducting pores during a large Na-dSpike.
source: The affinity of the sensor would need to be relatively low, in order to respond only to the high calcium concentration near the calcium-conducting pores during a large Na-dSpike.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for the proposed calcium sensor mechanism.

claim: The calcium sensor would need high cooperativity in order to respond selectively during the dSpike.
source: As our model predicts a modest increase in peak ICa (proportional to local calcium concentration) during a dSpike, relative to the slow synaptic depolarization, it is likely that the sensor would also need high cooperativity in order to respond selectively during the dSpike.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for the proposed calcium sensor mechanism based on the modeling results.

claim: Calmodulin may have the properties necessary to serve as the calcium sensor for LTP induction, namely low affinity, rapid binding kinetics, and high cooperativity for calcium binding.
source: The identities of the calcium sensors and the downstream biochemistry leading to LTP induction are the subjects of ongoing research (Amici et al., 2009), but calmodulin may have the properties necessary to serve this function, namely low affinity, rapid binding kinetics, and high cooperativity for calcium binding (Faas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known properties of calmodulin and citations to previous literature.

claim: Calmodulin has been postulated to be the initial calcium sensor coupled to other key LTP-inducing molecules such as calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II.
source: Calmodulin has been postulated to be the initial calcium sensor coupled to other key LTP-inducing molecules such as calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (Bradshaw et al., 2003; Lisman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The block of LTP by intracellular calcium buffering suggests that NMDAR and L-Cav channels contribute to the induction of PP→CA1tuft LTP by their ionotropic rather than metabotropic functions.
source: However, the block of LTP by intracellular calcium buffering (Figure 9) suggests that NMDAR and L-Cav channels contribute to the induction of PP → CA1tuft LTP by their ionotropic rather than metabotropic functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that calcium buffering blocks LTP.

claim: The lack of effect of nimodipine on synaptic responses after LTP induction indicates that the effect of nimodipine on TBS-induced PP→CA1tuft LTP cannot be explained by the block of a presynaptic expression mechanism mediated by L-Cav channels.
source: Moreover, high-frequency stimulation of PP → CA1tuft synapses has been shown to result in LTP expression mediated by functional upregulation of presynaptic Cav channels (Ahmed and Siegelbaum, 2009), but the lack of effect of nimodipine on synaptic responses after LTP induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicates that the effect of nimodipine on TBS-induced PP → CA1tuft LTP cannot be explained by the block of a presynaptic expression mechanism mediated by L-Cav channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The requirement for Na-dSpikes has interesting functional implications for PP→CA1tuft LTP, including potential compartmentalization of plasticity to individual dendritic branches.
source: The requirement for Na-dSpikes has interesting functional implications for PP → CA1tuft LTP. The activation of multiple synapses on a single dendritic branch leads to initiation of a dSpike (Losonczy and Magee, 2006), but dSpikes tend to fail at branch points (Spruston, 2008; Katz et al., 2009). Thus, the spatial extent of a Na-dSpike-dependent LTP event may be restricted to a particular dendritic branch, or even a segment of a branch containing the synapses that contribute to initiation of a Na-dSpike.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and citations to previous literature on dendritic spike propagation.

claim: Compartmentalization of plasticity to individual dendritic branches would have substantial implications for the granularity of associations learned at the dendritic level and the information-carrying capacity of a pyramidal neuron.
source: If true, such compartmentalization of plasticity (Losonczy et al., 2008; Makara et al., 2009; Makino and Malinow, 2011) would have substantial implications for the granularity of associations learned at the dendritic level, and consequently, the information-carrying capacity of a pyramidal neuron, as information may be stored discretely in individual dendritic branches or segments, rather than in an entire neuron (Poirazi and Mel, 2001; Mehta, 2004; Wu and Mel, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results and citations to previous literature.

claim: There are many forms of LTP, so it is not clear how general the requirement for Na-dSpikes will prove to be.
source: There are many forms of LTP, so it is not clear how general the requirement for Na-dSpikes will prove to be, even at the same synapses but with a different induction protocol.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the diversity of LTP mechanisms and the limitations of generalizing the current findings.

claim: LTP has been induced at SC synapses on CA1 pyramidal neurons using protocols that produce synaptic depolarization alone, without bAPs or dSpikes.
source: For example, LTP has been induced at SC synapses on CA1 pyramidal neurons using many different protocols, such as those that produce synaptic depolarization alone, without bAPs or dSpikes (Gustafsson et al., 1987; Isaac et al., 1995; Liao et al., 1995; Han and Heinemann, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A form of LTP at SC synapses depends on an instructive signal from coincident PP activation and is mediated by endocannabinoid release from dendrites.
source: Another interesting form of LTP at SC synapses depends on an instructive signal from coincident PP activation (Dudman et al., 2007). This form of LTP does not depend on bAPs or dSpikes either, but is mediated by endocannabinoid release from dendrites, induced by summation of EPSPs from both pathways, which ultimately downregulates feedforward inhibition (Xu et al., 2012; Basu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other forms of LTP at SC synapses have been reported to depend on postsynaptic action potential firing, presumably via bAPs.
source: At these same SC synapses, other forms of LTP have been reported to depend on postsynaptic action potential firing, presumably via bAPs (Magee and Johnston, 1997; Thomas et al., 1998; Wittenberg and Wang, 2006; Buchanan and Mellor, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other forms of LTP at SC synapses are correlated with the initiation of dSpikes, but it is unclear what role Na-dSpikes play, relative to Ca-dSpikes or NMDA-dSpikes.
source: Still other forms of LTP at SC synapses, however, are correlated with the initiation of dSpikes (Remy and Spruston, 2007; Hardie and Spruston, 2009), but it is unclear what role Na-dSpikes play, relative to Ca-dSpikes or NMDA-dSpikes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rhythmic whisker stimulation induced LTP in somatosensory cortex, even when the stimulus did not drive somatic action potential firing.
source: Importantly, however, a recent study demonstrated that rhythmic whisker stimulation induced LTP in somatosensory cortex, even when the stimulus did not drive somatic action potential firing (Gambino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: LTP can occur in vivo, in response to naturalistic stimulation, even in the absence of axo-somatic spiking.
source: Thus, LTP can occur in vivo, in response to naturalistic simulation, even in the absence of axo-somatic spiking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the citation to Gambino et al., 2014.

claim: The diversity of LTP induction mechanisms is likely to contribute to the powerful learning capacity of the brain.
source: The diversity of LTP induction mechanisms is likely to contribute to the powerful learning capacity of the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the understanding of the diversity of LTP mechanisms.

claim: Dendritic Nav channels were previously known to contribute to the cellular basis of memory by mediating forms of LTP that require action potential backpropagation, implementing the Hebbian plasticity rule 'neurons that fire together wire together'.
source: Dendritic Nav channels were previously known to contribute to the cellular basis of memory by mediating forms of LTP that require action potential backpropagation. In this case, the Hebbian plasticity rule—'neurons that fire together wire together'—is implemented by bAPs.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The form of LTP studied here implements a Hebbian plasticity rule on a finer spatial scale, which can be rephrased as 'neurites that fire together wire together'.
source: Our view is that this form of LTP is Hebbian on a finer spatial scale, for which the rule can be rephrased as 'neurites that fire together wire together'. Dendritic Nav channels play a central role in the cellular implementation of this rule, by determining which postsynaptic neurites fire.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of Hebbian learning theory.
